reason: The text explicitly contradicts this statement through multiple elements. Most directly, when Jehoshaphat establishes judicial reforms, he states that God shows no partiality, favoritism, or bias toward the elite: 'There is no iniquity with the LORD our God, nor partiality, nor taking of bribes' (אֵ֞ין עִם־ יְהוָ֣ה אֱלֹהֵ֗ינוּ עַוְלָ֛ה וּמַשֹּׂ֥א פָנִ֖ים וּמִקַּח־ שֹֽׁחַד). The narrative also demonstrates the fallibility of the powerful: 400 elite prophets deliver false prophecies, while the solitary prophet Micaiah speaks God's truth. The judges are explicitly instructed to judge for God, not for people—establishing that justice must be blind to status. Furthermore, the text emphasizes that all are subject to God's law equally, rejecting any notion of inherent superiority based on social position.
